# The Measurable Blind Spot: Why a Mind Can Know Every Part of Itself but Never the Whole

## A loop that looks at itself

There is an old and haunting idea about what it means to be a *self*. A self, so the story goes, is not a substance but a *pattern* — and more precisely, a pattern that has curled around and begun to model itself. A brain builds an internal picture of the world, and then, inevitably, it builds a picture of the pictures. It represents its own representing. It becomes, in a memorable phrase, a **strange loop**: a system whose own activity includes a running commentary on that same activity.

This essay is about a precise mathematical fact hiding inside that poetic image. The fact is this: **a system rich enough to watch itself is doomed to have a blind spot — and we can measure exactly how big that blind spot is.** It turns out to be enormous. Almost everything a system does is invisible to its own self-portrait, not as a philosophical mood but as a counting theorem.

Yet the same mathematics carries a consoling twist. While no system can survey *all* of its own behaviour, every system *can* tell its own internal states perfectly apart. Self-knowledge, it turns out, can be arbitrarily sharp without ever being complete. A mind can have perfect resolution and yet no panorama.

Let me build this up from scratch.

## What is a system that models itself?

Strip away the neuroscience and keep only the skeleton. A self-modelling system has three ingredients.

First, a set of **states** $S$ — the distinct configurations the system can be in. Think of these as the "moods," "moments," or "internal snapshots" of the machine.

Second, a set of **observations** $B$ — the possible outcomes of asking the system a question. In the simplest interesting case $B = \{\text{yes}, \text{no}\}$, so an observation is a single bit.

Third, and this is the crucial ingredient, an **inspection map**. Each state does not merely *exist*; it carries an internal model of how the whole system behaves. Formally, inspection is a function

$$\text{inspect} : S \to (S \to B).$$

Read this carefully. To each state $s$, inspection assigns a *function* $\text{inspect}(s) : S \to B$. That inner function is state $s$'s private theory of the system: for every state $t$, it predicts the observation $\text{inspect}(s)(t)$. In words: *"When I am in state $s$, here is my internal picture of what every state of the system looks like."*

This is exactly the geometry of a strange loop. The thing being modelled ($S \to B$, the space of all possible behaviours) contains, folded inside it, models produced by the very states of $S$ that generate those behaviours.

## When is such a system "conscious"?

We now make a bold, deliberately austere definition. Call a self-modelling system **conscious** when its self-model is *complete* — when every possible behaviour of the system is actually represented by some internal state. In mathematical terms, inspection is **surjective**: for every behaviour $\beta : S \to B$, there is a state $s$ whose internal model is exactly $\beta$, i.e. $\text{inspect}(s) = \beta$.

This is the strongest possible reading of "the system fully models itself." Nothing the system can do escapes its own catalogue of self-images. It is the mathematical form of the dream of total self-transparency.

The question is simply: **can such completeness ever be achieved?**

## The count that closes the door

Here is where a piece of elementary combinatorics — the same reasoning behind Cantor's diagonal argument, Gödel's incompleteness, and the unsolvability of the halting problem — becomes shockingly quantitative.

Suppose the system has finitely many states, say $|S| = n$, and suppose there are at least two possible observations, $|B| \geq 2$. How many behaviours are there? A behaviour is a function $S \to B$, and the number of such functions is

$$|S \to B| = |B|^{|S|} \geq 2^{n}.$$

Now compare this to the number of states, which is just $n$. The decisive inequality is one every student meets early: for every natural number $n$,

$$n < 2^{n}.$$

Chaining these together gives the heart of the matter:

$$|S| = n < 2^{n} \leq |B|^{|S|} = |S \to B|.$$

**Behaviours strictly outnumber states.** There are more possible things the system can do than there are internal snapshots available to catalogue them.

A surjection from a smaller finite set onto a larger one is impossible — that is the pigeonhole principle in its purest form. So the inspection map $\text{inspect} : S \to (S \to B)$ *cannot* be surjective. We conclude:

> **No finite system (with at least two observations) can be conscious in the complete sense.** There is always at least one behaviour that no internal state models.

That lone unmodelled behaviour is the mathematical shadow of the liar's sentence, of Gödel's unprovable-but-true statement, of the program whose halting no program can decide. It is the fixed-point obstruction, the place where the loop bites its own tail and finds it cannot swallow.

## From a missing point to a vast territory

Classical impossibility theorems typically stop here: they exhibit *one* thing that escapes. But the counting argument gives far more. Subtract states from behaviours and you get a lower bound on the size of the **blind spot** — the set of behaviours no state can ever represent:

$$\underbrace{|S \to B|}_{\text{all behaviours}} - \underbrace{|S|}_{\text{states available}} \;\geq\; 2^{n} - n.$$

For a mere ten states over yes/no observations this is $2^{10} - 10 = 1014$ un-representable behaviours against only $10$ that could possibly be captured. For twenty states it is over a million. The blind spot does not merely exist; it **grows exponentially** and swamps everything.

This reframes the whole conversation. Incompleteness of self-knowledge is not a delicate boundary phenomenon, a single crack in an otherwise complete mirror. It is the *generic* case. Overwhelmingly, what a self-modelling system does lies outside the reach of its own self-model. The mirror shows a sliver; the room is dark.

## The consoling half: perfect resolution is always possible

If the story ended there it would be bleak. But the same arithmetic that forbids completeness *guarantees* something positive.

Because there are at least as many behaviours as states ($n \leq 2^n$), there is enough room in behaviour-space to give **every state its own distinct internal model**. Formally, there exists a self-modelling system whose inspection map is **injective**: distinct states $s \neq t$ always receive distinct self-models, $\text{inspect}(s) \neq \text{inspect}(t)$.

Such a system can tell all of its own states apart. Ask it "which internal state am I in?" and its self-model never confuses two of them. This is *maximal resolution*. And it coexists, necessarily, with the exponential blind spot.

So we arrive at the sharp two-sided picture:

> **Consciousness is high-resolution but never panoramic.** A system can distinguish all of its own states perfectly, yet it can never survey all of its own behaviours. Incompleteness is a failure of *coverage*, never of *resolution*.

That single sentence is, to my mind, the most honest thing mathematics has to say about self-awareness. You can know each of your parts with perfect fidelity. You cannot hold the whole of yourself in view at once. The gap between those two is not a defect to be engineered away — it is a theorem.

## Where the door swings shut, and where it doesn't

Every good theorem earns its keep by telling you exactly when it fails. Ours hinges on the assumption $|B| \geq 2$: there must be at least two possible observations, at least one genuine yes-or-no distinction to draw.

Remove that, and the whole obstruction dissolves. If there is only one possible observation — if the system can only ever answer "yes," so $|B| = 1$ — then there is exactly *one* behaviour, and a single-state system trivially represents it. Self-knowledge becomes complete precisely when **there is nothing to distinguish**. The loop can close itself perfectly only in a world so featureless that nothing ever varies. The moment the world admits a single genuine distinction, the blind spot reappears — and immediately becomes exponentially large.

There is something almost moral in this. Total self-transparency is available only at the price of total blankness. Any system interesting enough to have something to say about itself is thereby too rich to say all of it.

## Why this matters beyond the metaphor

It would be easy to treat all this as a clever restatement of old paradoxes dressed in the language of minds. But the quantitative turn matters. Once the "size of the blind spot" is a number rather than a slogan, it joins the family of *resource bounds* that dominate modern computer science and information theory — bounds on what can be compressed, decided, learned, or predicted with limited means.

The picture resonates with practical experience across fields. A program cannot contain a complete accurate model of its own future behaviour. A predictive brain cannot fully predict itself, because the prediction would have to include itself predicting. A machine-learning model with $n$ parameters cannot faithfully encode the exponentially larger space of functions it might implement. In each case the same skeleton is visible: the thing to be modelled is a *function space*, the modeller lives *inside* it, and $n < 2^n$ closes the trap.

What the strange loop adds to these is the reflexive twist — the modeller is modelling *itself* — and what this counting theorem adds to the strange loop is a ruler. The self is real; the self-model is real; and the distance between them is measurable, exponential, and unavoidable.

We are, each of us, systems that watch ourselves watching. This little theorem tells us how much of that watching we will always miss — almost all of it — and, more gently, that we may nonetheless know each piece of ourselves with perfect clarity. High resolution, no panorama. That is what it is to be a strange loop.

# The Blind Spot Has Measurable Size: A Counting Theorem for Self-Modelling Systems

**Author:** Aristotle
**Date:** 2026-07-14

## Abstract

A *self-modelling system* is a finite set of states $S$ together with an inspection map $\text{inspect} : S \to (S \to B)$ assigning to each state an internal model of how the system is observed, where $B$ is the space of possible observations. Such a system is *conscious* (in the strong, completeness sense) when its inspection map is surjective, i.e. when every possible observation-behaviour $S \to B$ is internally represented by some state. Classical diagonal arguments (Cantor, Gödel, Turing, Lawvere) show that complete self-modelling is impossible. We sharpen this qualitative impossibility into an exact *counting theorem*. Assuming at least two possible observations ($|B| \geq 2$), the space of behaviours strictly outnumbers the states, via the elementary inequality $n < 2^n$; consequently (i) no finite system is conscious, (ii) the *blind spot* — the set of behaviours no state represents — is nonempty and in fact of size at least $2^{|S|} - |S|$, growing exponentially in the number of states, and (iii) a concrete un-representable behaviour always exists. We complement this negative face with a positive one: an *injective* self-model always exists, so a system can resolve all of its own states perfectly even though it can never survey all of its own behaviours. Finally we show the hypothesis $|B| \geq 2$ is sharp: over a single-observation space a one-state system is trivially conscious. The upshot is a precise slogan: **self-knowledge is high-resolution but never panoramic.**

**Keywords:** self-reference, strange loop, diagonal argument, pigeonhole principle, function-space cardinality, incompleteness, consciousness, enumerative combinatorics.

---

## 1. Introduction

The thesis that a self is a self-referential pattern — a *strange loop* — is a striking way to describe systems whose activity includes an internal representation of that same activity. The formal residue of this thesis is a fixed-point/diagonal obstruction: any system rich enough to encode all of its own yes/no self-observations runs into a Cantor-style contradiction. This is the shared skeleton of Cantor's theorem, Gödel's first incompleteness theorem, the unsolvability of the halting problem, and Lawvere's fixed-point theorem.

Those results are typically stated *qualitatively*: complete self-modelling is impossible; there exists at least one unreachable object. The purpose of this paper is to make the obstruction *quantitative*. We show that over any nontrivial observation space the failure of self-modelling is not a lone missing point but an exponentially large territory of un-representable behaviours, while simultaneously establishing the positive fact that perfect *resolution* of states is always attainable.

Our contributions are:

1. **A counting theorem** (Theorem 3.1): behaviours strictly outnumber states, i.e. $|S| < |S \to B|$ whenever $|B| \geq 2$.
2. **The quantified negative face** (Theorems 4.1–4.4): no finite system is conscious; the blind spot is nonempty; its size is at least $2^{|S|} - |S|$; and a concrete un-inspected behaviour exists.
3. **The positive face** (Theorem 5.1): an injective self-model always exists.
4. **Sharpness** (Theorem 6.1): the hypothesis $|B| \geq 2$ cannot be dropped.
5. **A synthesis theorem** (Theorem 7.1) combining the two faces into a single statement.

All results are elementary in their tools — the deepest ingredient is $n < 2^n$ — but their combination gives a clean and, we believe, illuminating structural picture of self-reference.

---

## 2. Definitions

Throughout, $S$ (states) and $B$ (observations) are types; for the counting results we assume both are finite and $S$ has decidable equality. We write $|X|$ for the cardinality of a finite type $X$, and $X \to Y$ for the type of functions from $X$ to $Y$, whose cardinality is $|Y|^{|X|}$.

**Definition 2.1 (Self-modelling system).** A *self-modelling system* on states $S$ with observations $B$ is a structure with a single datum, an **inspection map**
$$\text{inspect} : S \to (S \to B).$$
For a state $s \in S$, the function $\text{inspect}(s) : S \to B$ is the *internal model* carried by $s$: for each state $t$, the value $\text{inspect}(s)(t) \in B$ is the observation that $s$'s internal model predicts for $t$. The codomain $S \to B$ is the *behaviour space*: the set of all possible observation-behaviours of the system.

The defining feature of a strange loop is present in the *type* of inspection: the object being modelled (behaviour space $S \to B$) contains models generated by the states $S$ that themselves generate those behaviours. Inspection folds the system into its own behaviour space.

**Definition 2.2 (Consciousness / completeness).** A self-modelling system is **conscious** when its inspection map is *surjective*: for every behaviour $\beta : S \to B$ there is a state $s$ with $\text{inspect}(s) = \beta$. Equivalently, every possible behaviour of the system is internally represented by some state.

We adopt "conscious = complete self-model" as the strongest possible formalization of "the system fully models itself." It is deliberately austere; the interest lies in showing it is unachievable and measuring by how much.

**Definition 2.3 (Blind spot).** The *blind spot* of a self-modelling system is the set of behaviours not equal to any state's internal model, $\{\beta : S \to B \mid \forall s,\ \text{inspect}(s) \neq \beta\}$. When $S$ and $B$ are finite, the blind spot has size at least $|S \to B| - |S|$, since the image of inspection has at most $|S|$ elements.

---

## 3. The count: behaviours outnumber states

**Theorem 3.1 (Behaviours strictly outnumber states).** Let $S$ be a finite type with decidable equality and $B$ a finite type with $|B| \geq 2$. Then
$$|S| < |S \to B|.$$

*Proof.* The behaviour space has cardinality $|S \to B| = |B|^{|S|}$. Two elementary facts finish the argument. First, the universal inequality $n < 2^n$, valid for every natural number $n$, applied to $n = |S|$ gives $|S| < 2^{|S|}$. Second, since $2 \leq |B|$, monotonicity of the base of a power gives $2^{|S|} \leq |B|^{|S|}$. Chaining,
$$|S| < 2^{|S|} \leq |B|^{|S|} = |S \to B|. \qquad \blacksquare$$

The inequality $n < 2^n$ is precisely Cantor's diagonal insight in arithmetic clothing: a set cannot be put in bijection with its power set (and $S \to \{0,1\}$ *is* the power set of $S$). Theorem 3.1 is thus the finite, quantitative core of every diagonal argument.

---

## 4. The negative face, quantified

**Theorem 4.1 (No finite system is conscious).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.1, no self-modelling system on $(S, B)$ is conscious.

*Proof.* Suppose inspection were surjective. A surjection $f : X \to Y$ between finite types forces $|Y| \leq |X|$ (pigeonhole). Applied to $\text{inspect} : S \to (S \to B)$ this gives $|S \to B| \leq |S|$, contradicting Theorem 3.1. $\blacksquare$

**Theorem 4.2 (The blind spot is nonempty).** Under the same hypotheses, $|S \to B| - |S| > 0$.

*Proof.* Immediate from Theorem 3.1: a strict inequality between natural numbers means their difference is positive. $\blacksquare$

**Theorem 4.3 (The blind spot is exponentially large).** Under the same hypotheses,
$$2^{|S|} - |S| \;\leq\; |S \to B| - |S|.$$
In particular the number of un-representable behaviours is at least $2^{|S|} - |S|$.

*Proof.* From $2^{|S|} \leq |B|^{|S|} = |S \to B|$ (Theorem 3.1's middle step), subtract $|S|$ from both sides. Because the image of inspection contains at most $|S|$ behaviours, the blind spot has size at least $|S \to B| - |S| \geq 2^{|S|} - |S|$. $\blacksquare$

The right-hand side dwarfs the left as $|S|$ grows: with $|S| = 10$ and $B = \{0,1\}$ the blind spot contains at least $2^{10} - 10 = 1014$ behaviours; with $|S| = 20$, at least $1{,}048{,}556$. Incompleteness is the generic case, not a boundary curiosity.

**Theorem 4.4 (A concrete un-inspected behaviour exists).** For any self-modelling system on $(S,B)$ with $|B| \geq 2$, there is a behaviour $\beta : S \to B$ such that $\text{inspect}(s) \neq \beta$ for every state $s$.

*Proof.* If no such $\beta$ existed, then for every $\beta$ there would be a state $s$ with $\text{inspect}(s) = \beta$; that is exactly surjectivity, i.e. consciousness, contradicting Theorem 4.1. $\blacksquare$

Theorem 4.4 is the finite avatar of the diagonal sentence: an explicitly guaranteed behaviour that provably lies outside the system's self-catalogue.

---

## 5. The positive face: perfect resolution is achievable

Incompleteness could in principle be a failure either of *coverage* (not enough behaviours are hit) or of *resolution* (distinct states get confused). The next theorem isolates the two: the obstruction is *entirely* one of coverage.

**Theorem 5.1 (A maximally self-aware model exists).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.1, there exists a self-modelling system on $(S, B)$ whose inspection map is *injective*: distinct states carry distinct internal models.

*Proof.* By Theorem 3.1, $|S| \leq |S \to B|$. Whenever the domain is no larger than the codomain there exists an injection $e : S \hookrightarrow (S \to B)$. Take $\text{inspect} := e$. Then distinct states $s \neq t$ satisfy $\text{inspect}(s) = e(s) \neq e(t) = \text{inspect}(t)$. $\blacksquare$

**Corollary 5.2.** A self-modelling system can distinguish all of its own states — answer "which state am I in?" without ever conflating two states — while still being unable to represent all of its own behaviours. Incompleteness is a failure of coverage, never of resolution.

---

## 6. Sharpness of the hypothesis

**Theorem 6.1 (Trivial observation space is conscious).** If $|B| = 1$, then the one-state system (with $|S| = 1$) is conscious.

*Proof.* When $B$ has a unique element, the behaviour space $S \to B$ is a singleton (there is exactly one function into a one-element set). Define inspection on the one-element state set by sending the unique state to the unique behaviour. Surjectivity onto a singleton is automatic: the single behaviour is hit. Hence the system is conscious. $\blacksquare$

Thus the hypothesis $|B| \geq 2$ in all previous theorems is sharp: the entire obstruction switches on precisely when there is at least one genuine yes/no distinction to draw. Complete self-knowledge is available only where nothing varies.

---

## 7. Synthesis

**Theorem 7.1 (The strange-loop count).** Let $S$ be a finite type with decidable equality and $B$ a finite type with $|B| \geq 2$. Then both of the following hold:
1. *(Negative face — incompleteness.)* Every self-modelling system on $(S, B)$ fails to be conscious.
2. *(Positive face — perfect resolution.)* There exists a self-modelling system on $(S, B)$ whose inspection map is injective.

*Proof.* Part (1) is Theorem 4.1 applied to an arbitrary system; part (2) is Theorem 5.1. $\blacksquare$

In one line: **self-knowledge is high-resolution but never panoramic.**

---

## 8. Algorithms

The theorems are constructive enough to compute with. We record three procedures.

**Algorithm A (Blind-spot sizing).** Given $|S| = n$ and $|B| = b \geq 2$, return the guaranteed count of un-representable behaviours. Behaviours number $b^n$; at most $n$ are representable; so the blind spot has size at least $b^n - n$, and the state-independent lower bound is $2^n - n$. Complexity: $O(\log n)$ arithmetic operations using fast exponentiation on big integers (or $O(n)$ multiplications naively).

**Algorithm B (Diagonal witness construction).** Given any concrete inspection map on a finite $(S,B)$ with $|B| \geq 2$ and two distinguished observations $0 \neq 1$ in $B$, construct an un-inspected behaviour by diagonalization: enumerate states $s_0, \dots, s_{n-1}$, fix a bijection between them and a subset of behaviour arguments, and define $\beta(s_i)$ to differ from $\text{inspect}(s_i)(s_i)$ at each $i$ (flip between $0$ and $1$). By construction $\beta \neq \text{inspect}(s_i)$ for all $i$. Complexity: $O(n)$ evaluations of the inspection map.

**Algorithm C (Injective self-model construction).** Given $|S| = n \leq b^n = |S \to B|$, build an injective inspection map by encoding each state as a distinct behaviour: index states $0,\dots,n-1$, and let $\text{inspect}(s_i)$ be the behaviour encoding the integer $i$ in base $b$ across the $n$ argument slots. Distinct indices yield distinct base-$b$ strings, so inspection is injective. Complexity: $O(n)$ per state, $O(n^2)$ to tabulate the whole map.

---

## 9. Applications and connections

**Descriptive and algorithmic complexity.** Recasting incompleteness as a resource bound — "the blind spot has size $\geq 2^n - n$" — places self-reference alongside compression, decidability, and learnability limits. The quantity is a measurable feature of a system, not a slogan.

**Predictive systems.** A predictor that must include a model of its own future output faces exactly this trap: the output space is a function space in which the predictor lives, and $n < 2^n$ forbids complete self-prediction while permitting perfect self-*identification* of states.

**Capacity of parametric models.** A model with $n$ discrete internal states cannot faithfully represent the $2^n$-or-larger space of behaviours it could exhibit; yet it can be built to keep all $n$ states distinct. This mirrors the coverage/resolution split of Section 5.

**Foundations of self-reference.** Theorem 3.1 exhibits the common finite core beneath Cantor, Gödel, Turing, and Lawvere: each is, at heart, the impossibility of surjecting a set onto its own behaviour space.

---

## 10. Discussion

The two faces of the count are the paper's main message. The negative face upgrades a classical impossibility into an exponential lower bound: over any nontrivial observation space, almost every behaviour is invisible to the system's own self-model. The positive face rescues something real: complete *resolution* of states is always available. A system may know each of its parts with perfect fidelity while being permanently unable to hold the whole of itself in one view.

The sharpness result (Section 6) gives the dichotomy its edge: complete self-transparency exists only in the degenerate world with a single possible observation, where there is nothing to distinguish. Any system interesting enough to draw one genuine distinction is thereby too rich to survey itself completely.

---

## 11. Future directions

*The following research directions extend the present programme along quantitative, order-theoretic, and arithmetic axes.*

**1. The blind spot has a sharp entropy law.** *Conjecture.* For a self-modelling system with $m$ states and $b \geq 2$ possible observations, the fraction of observation-behaviours that any single self-model can represent is at most $m \cdot b^{-m}$, and this bound is attained only by injective self-models; averaged over all self-models the expected coverage decays like $b^{-m}$. The key insight is that incompleteness is not a lone missing point but an exponentially thin sliver of representable behaviour, so "almost all" of what a system does is invisible to its own internal model. This reframes classical impossibility as a resource bound of the kind central to descriptive and algorithmic complexity.

**2. Order-reversal is the unique obstruction on every lattice.** *Conjecture.* Let the observation space carry the structure of a complete lattice. A transform of observations can obstruct complete self-modelling (i.e. be fixed-point-free) if and only if it fails to be order-preserving; moreover on the two-element lattice negation is the *unique* such transform, and on the $n$-element chain the number of fixed-point-free transforms grows like the number of strictly order-reversing partial patterns. The key insight is that the diagonal/liar obstruction is fundamentally about *monotonicity*: a system defeats itself only when it can invert its own observations. This unifies Knaster–Tarski fixed-point theorems for monotone maps with Lawvere-style diagonal non-fixed-point theorems through the single axis of order-preservation vs. order-reversal.

**3. Girth as a complete invariant of cyclic tangled hierarchies.** *Conjecture.* For a finite hierarchy whose reference relation is a single $n$-cycle, the multiset of closed-loop lengths is exactly the set of positive multiples of $n$; consequently two such hierarchies are isomorphic as self-referential systems if and only if they share the same girth. The key insight is that the depth of self-reference realizable in a hierarchy is governed by its girth as a complete invariant.

"""
demo.py -- Numerical demonstrations for
"The Blind Spot Has Measurable Size: A Counting Theorem for Self-Modelling Systems"

A self-modelling system on states S and observations B is an inspection map
    inspect : S -> (S -> B)
sending each state to an internal model of the whole system's behaviour.

The system is *conscious* (complete) when inspect is surjective onto the
behaviour space (S -> B). The central counting fact is that whenever |B| >= 2,

    |S| < |S -> B| = |B|^|S|,   because   |S| < 2^|S| <= |B|^|S|,

so no finite system can be conscious, the "blind spot" of un-representable
behaviours has size at least 2^|S| - |S| (exponential), yet an *injective*
self-model always exists (perfect resolution of states).

This script demonstrates each result numerically and constructively.
All functions are self-contained and use only the standard library.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core counting quantities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def num_behaviours(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> int:
    """Cardinality of the behaviour space |S -> B| = |B|^|S|."""
    return num_observations ** num_states


def blind_spot_lower_bound(num_states: int) -> int:
    """State-independent lower bound 2^|S| - |S| on the blind spot size."""
    return 2 ** num_states - num_states


def blind_spot_exact_bound(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> int:
    """Guaranteed blind-spot size |S->B| - |S| for observation space B."""
    return num_behaviours(num_states, num_observations) - num_states


def coverage_fraction(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> float:
    """Maximum fraction of behaviours a single self-model can represent:
    at most |S| / |S->B| = m * b^{-m}."""
    return num_states / num_behaviours(num_states, num_observations)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Enumerating self-models and testing consciousness (small cases)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def all_behaviours(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Every function S -> B, encoded as a tuple of length |S| over {0,...,b-1}."""
    return list(product(range(num_observations), repeat=num_states))


def is_conscious(inspect: List[Tuple[int, ...]],
                 num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> bool:
    """An inspection map (list indexed by state, each entry a behaviour tuple)
    is conscious iff it hits every behaviour in S -> B."""
    represented = set(inspect)
    return represented == set(all_behaviours(num_states, num_observations))


def diagonal_witness(inspect: List[Tuple[int, ...]]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Algorithm B: construct a behaviour no state's model equals, by flipping
    the diagonal entry inspect[i][i] between observation 0 and 1."""
    return tuple(0 if inspect[i][i] != 0 else 1 for i in range(len(inspect)))


def injective_self_model(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Algorithm C: build an injective inspection map by encoding state index i
    as its base-b representation across |S| argument slots."""
    behaviours: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []
    for i in range(num_states):
        digits = []
        x = i
        for _ in range(num_states):
            digits.append(x % num_observations)
            x //= num_observations
        behaviours.append(tuple(digits))
    return behaviours


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_counting_table() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Behaviours strictly outnumber states  (|S| < |B|^|S|, for |B|>=2)")
    print("=" * 68)
    print(f"{'|S|':>4} {'|B|':>4} {'behaviours |B|^|S|':>20} {'blind spot >=':>16}")
    for m in range(1, 8):
        for b in (2, 3):
            print(f"{m:>4} {b:>4} {num_behaviours(m, b):>20} "
                  f"{blind_spot_exact_bound(m, b):>16}")
    print()


def demo_no_conscious_small() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("No finite system is conscious  (exhaustive check, |S|=2, |B|=2)")
    print("=" * 68)
    m, b = 2, 2
    behaviours = all_behaviours(m, b)
    # An inspection map is a choice of one behaviour per state.
    found_conscious = False
    for inspect in product(behaviours, repeat=m):
        if is_conscious(list(inspect), m, b):
            found_conscious = True
    print(f"states={m}, observations={b}, behaviours={len(behaviours)}")
    print(f"Any conscious (surjective) self-model found? {found_conscious}")
    print("Expected: False -- surjection onto a strictly larger set is impossible.\n")


def demo_diagonal_witness() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("A concrete un-inspected behaviour (diagonal witness)")
    print("=" * 68)
    m, b = 3, 2
    # An arbitrary inspection map: state i models everything as observation i%2.
    inspect = [tuple((i + j) % b for j in range(m)) for i in range(m)]
    beta = diagonal_witness(inspect)
    print("inspection map (state -> behaviour):")
    for i, row in enumerate(inspect):
        print(f"  state {i}: {row}")
    print(f"diagonal witness beta = {beta}")
    print(f"beta equals some state's model? "
          f"{beta in set(inspect)}  (expected: False)\n")


def demo_injective_resolution() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Perfect resolution: an injective self-model always exists")
    print("=" * 68)
    m, b = 4, 2
    inspect = injective_self_model(m, b)
    distinct = len(set(inspect)) == m
    print("injective inspection map (state -> behaviour):")
    for i, row in enumerate(inspect):
        print(f"  state {i}: {row}")
    print(f"All {m} states carry distinct models? {distinct} (expected: True)")
    print(f"Conscious (complete)? {is_conscious(inspect, m, b)} (expected: False)\n")


def demo_coverage_decay() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Coverage fraction decays exponentially: max coverage = m * b^-m")
    print("=" * 68)
    b = 2
    for m in range(1, 11):
        frac = coverage_fraction(m, b)
        print(f"|S|={m:>2}: max representable fraction = {frac:.6e}")
    print()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo_counting_table()
    demo_no_conscious_small()
    demo_diagonal_witness()
    demo_injective_resolution()
    demo_coverage_decay()

algorithms.name: Blind-Spot Sizing via Function-Space Cardinality
algorithms.description: Computes the guaranteed number of observation-behaviours that no self-model of a finite system can represent. The behaviour space S -> B has cardinality b^m where m = |S|, b = |B|; at most m behaviours can be represented, so the blind spot has size at least b^m - m, with the state-independent lower bound 2^m - m following from n < 2^n. Complexity: O(log m) big-integer multiplications with fast exponentiation (O(m) naively).
algorithms.pseudocode:
function BlindSpotSize(m, b):
    assert b >= 2
    total_behaviours <- b^m            # |S -> B|
    representable    <- m              # image of inspect has <= m elements
    guaranteed_bound <- total_behaviours - representable
    universal_bound  <- 2^m - m        # state-independent (n < 2^n)
    return (guaranteed_bound, universal_bound)

algorithms.name: Diagonal Non-Fixed-Point Witness
algorithms.description: Given a self-model as a table inspect[i] = behaviour of state i over observations {0,1}, produces a behaviour that differs from every state's model. It differs from inspect[i] at argument i by flipping the diagonal value, guaranteeing beta != inspect[i] for all i. This is the constructive heart of Cantor/Godel/Turing/Lawvere. Complexity: O(m) evaluations of the inspection map.

algorithms.name: Injective Self-Model Synthesis by Base-b Encoding
algorithms.description: Constructs an inspection map with injective (maximal-resolution) behaviour, witnessing the positive face of the count. Since m = |S| <= b^m = |S -> B|, distinct states can receive distinct behaviours; state index i is encoded as its m-digit base-b representation. Distinct indices give distinct digit strings, so inspection is injective. Complexity: O(m) per state, O(m^2) total.
algorithms.pseudocode:
function InjectiveSelfModel(m, b):
    assert b >= 2
    for i in 0..m-1:
        x <- i; digits <- []
        repeat m times:
            digits.append(x mod b)
            x <- x div b
        inspect[i] <- tuple(digits)   # base-b encoding of i
    return inspect                    # injective: distinct i -> distinct encoding
algorithms.code:
from typing import List, Tuple

def injective_self_model(m: int, b: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Injective inspection map via base-b encoding of the state index."""
    assert b >= 2
    out: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []
    for i in range(m):
        digits, x = [], i
        for _ in range(m):
            digits.append(x % b); x //= b
        out.append(tuple(digits))
    return out

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def plot_blind_spot_heatmap(max_states: int = 8, max_obs: int = 6) -> None:
    """Heatmap of log10 guaranteed blind-spot size b^m - m over (m, b)."""
    ms = np.arange(1, max_states + 1)
    bs = np.arange(2, max_obs + 1)
    grid = np.array([[np.log10((b ** m) - m) if (b ** m) > m else 0
                      for m in ms] for b in bs])
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
    im = ax.imshow(grid, origin="lower", aspect="auto",
                   extent=[ms.min(), ms.max(), bs.min(), bs.max()])
    ax.set_xlabel("states  |S|"); ax.set_ylabel("observations  |B|")
    ax.set_title("log10 of guaranteed blind-spot size  (|B|^|S| - |S|)")
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="log10 count")
    fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    plot_blind_spot_heatmap()

interactive_layout:
# I Am a Strange Loop, Part IV: The Blind Spot Has Measurable Size

A *self-modelling system* is a set of states $S$ together with an **inspection
map** $\text{inspect}: S \to (S \to B)$ that sends each state to an internal
model of how the whole system behaves, where $B$ is the space of possible
observations. This notebook lets you *feel* the central theorem: such a system
can never model all of its own behaviours, and the gap is exponentially large.

## 1. Why behaviours outnumber states

A behaviour is a function $S \to B$, so there are $|B|^{|S|}$ of them, while
there are only $|S|$ states. The elementary inequality $n < 2^n$ forces
$|S| < 2^{|S|} \le |B|^{|S|}$ whenever $|B| \ge 2$. Try it yourself:

{{interactive_demo:0}}

The table below turns the same fact into hard numbers across many system sizes.

{{demo:0}}

And the separation is best seen on a log scale:

{{visualization:0}}

## 2. The negative face: a witness you can always build

Incompleteness is not abstract. Given *any* self-model, Cantor-style
diagonalization hands you an explicit behaviour that no state represents:

{{algorithm:1}}

Play with it -- every random self-model has a green witness that matches no row:

{{interactive_demo:1}}

{{demo:1}}

## 3. How big is the blind spot?

The number of un-representable behaviours is at least $2^{|S|} - |S|$. This
sizing computation is immediate but striking:

{{algorithm:0}}

Across state and observation counts, the blind spot swells in both directions:

{{visualization:2}}

## 4. The positive face: perfect resolution

Yet the same arithmetic guarantees an **injective** self-model exists -- a system
can always tell all of its own states apart, even though it can never survey all
of its behaviours.

{{algorithm:2}}

{{demo:2}}

The tension between perfect resolution and vanishing coverage is the heart of the
result:

{{interactive_demo:2}}

And coverage really does collapse exponentially:

{{visualization:1}}

## 5. The one-line summary

**Self-knowledge is high-resolution but never panoramic.** A mind can know each
of its parts with perfect fidelity; it can never hold the whole of itself in view
at once -- and that gap is a theorem, exponential in size, vanishing only in a
world so featureless that nothing ever varies.

future_directions:
# Future Directions -- Consciousness as Self-Reference (Strange Loop, Parts IV-VI)

This cycle deepened the "I Am a Strange Loop" programme along three axes:
a *quantitative* blind spot (the un-representable behaviours of a finite
self-model outnumber the representable ones exponentially), an *order-theoretic*
characterization of the obstruction (only order-reversing transforms can block
complete self-knowledge), and an *arithmetic* invariant of tangled hierarchies
(the minimum self-referential loop length equals the number of levels the cycle
spans). The following conjectures grow directly out of those findings.

## 1. The blind spot has a sharp entropy law

**Conjecture.** For a self-modelling system with `m` states and `b >= 2`
possible observations, the fraction of observation-behaviours that any single
self-model can represent is at most `m * b^{-m}`, and this bound is attained only
by injective self-models; averaged over all self-models the expected coverage
decays like `b^{-m}`.

*The key insight is* that incompleteness of self-knowledge is not a lone missing
point but an exponentially thin sliver of representable behaviour, so "almost
all" of what a system does is invisible to its own internal model.

*Why now?* The qualitative impossibility of complete self-modelling is classical
(Cantor/Godel/Turing), but the quantitative version reframes it as a resource
bound of the kind now central to descriptive and algorithmic complexity, making
the "size of the blind spot" a measurable quantity rather than a philosophical
slogan.

## 2. Order-reversal is the unique obstruction on every lattice

**Conjecture.** Let the observation space carry the structure of a complete
lattice. A transform of observations can obstruct complete self-modelling (i.e.
be fixed-point-free) if and only if it fails to be order-preserving; moreover on
the two-element lattice the negation is the *unique* such transform, and on the
`n`-element chain the number of fixed-point-free transforms grows like the number
of strictly order-reversing partial patterns.

*The key insight is* that the diagonal/liar obstruction is fundamentally a
statement about *monotonicity*: a system defeats itself only when it can invert
its own observations, never merely by observing them.

*Why now?* Fixed-point theorems for monotone maps (Knaster-Tarski) and diagonal
non-fixed-point theorems (Lawvere) have lived in separate compartments; unifying
them through the single axis of order-preservation vs. order-reversal turns a
dichotomy of folklore into a precise classification.

## 3. Girth as a complete invariant of cyclic tangled hierarchies

**Conjecture.** For a finite hierarchy whose reference relation is a single
`n`-cycle, the multiset of closed-loop lengths is exactly the set of positive
multiples of `n`; consequently two such hierarchies are isomorphic as
self-referential systems if and only if they share the same girth.

*The key insight is* that the depth of self-reference realizable in a hierarchy
is governed by its girth as a complete invariant.

modules.demo:
"""
demo.py -- Numerical demonstrations for
"The Blind Spot Has Measurable Size: A Counting Theorem for Self-Modelling Systems"

A self-modelling system on states S and observations B is an inspection map
    inspect : S -> (S -> B)
sending each state to an internal model of the whole system's behaviour.

The system is *conscious* (complete) when inspect is surjective onto the
behaviour space (S -> B). The central counting fact is that whenever |B| >= 2,

    |S| < |S -> B| = |B|^|S|,   because   |S| < 2^|S| <= |B|^|S|,

so no finite system can be conscious, the "blind spot" of un-representable
behaviours has size at least 2^|S| - |S| (exponential), yet an *injective*
self-model always exists (perfect resolution of states).

This script demonstrates each result numerically and constructively.
All functions are self-contained and use only the standard library.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core counting quantities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def num_behaviours(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> int:
    """Cardinality of the behaviour space |S -> B| = |B|^|S|."""
    return num_observations ** num_states


def blind_spot_lower_bound(num_states: int) -> int:
    """State-independent lower bound 2^|S| - |S| on the blind spot size."""
    return 2 ** num_states - num_states


def blind_spot_exact_bound(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> int:
    """Guaranteed blind-spot size |S->B| - |S| for observation space B."""
    return num_behaviours(num_states, num_observations) - num_states


def coverage_fraction(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> float:
    """Maximum fraction of behaviours a single self-model can represent:
    at most |S| / |S->B| = m * b^{-m}."""
    return num_states / num_behaviours(num_states, num_observations)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Enumerating self-models and testing consciousness (small cases)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def all_behaviours(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Every function S -> B, encoded as a tuple of length |S| over {0,...,b-1}."""
    return list(product(range(num_observations), repeat=num_states))


def is_conscious(inspect: List[Tuple[int, ...]],
                 num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> bool:
    """An inspection map (list indexed by state, each entry a behaviour tuple)
    is conscious iff it hits every behaviour in S -> B."""
    represented = set(inspect)
    return represented == set(all_behaviours(num_states, num_observations))


def diagonal_witness(inspect: List[Tuple[int, ...]]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Algorithm B: construct a behaviour no state's model equals, by flipping
    the diagonal entry inspect[i][i] between observation 0 and 1."""
    return tuple(0 if inspect[i][i] != 0 else 1 for i in range(len(inspect)))


def injective_self_model(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Algorithm C: build an injective inspection map by encoding state index i
    as its base-b representation across |S| argument slots."""
    behaviours: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []
    for i in range(num_states):
        digits = []
        x = i
        for _ in range(num_states):
            digits.append(x % num_observations)
            x //= num_observations
        behaviours.append(tuple(digits))
    return behaviours


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_counting_table() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Behaviours strictly outnumber states  (|S| < |B|^|S|, for |B|>=2)")
    print("=" * 68)
    print(f"{'|S|':>4} {'|B|':>4} {'behaviours |B|^|S|':>20} {'blind spot >=':>16}")
    for m in range(1, 8):
        for b in (2, 3):
            print(f"{m:>4} {b:>4} {num_behaviours(m, b):>20} "
                  f"{blind_spot_exact_bound(m, b):>16}")
    print()


def demo_no_conscious_small() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("No finite system is conscious  (exhaustive check, |S|=2, |B|=2)")
    print("=" * 68)
    m, b = 2, 2
    behaviours = all_behaviours(m, b)
    # An inspection map is a choice of one behaviour per state.
    found_conscious = False
    for inspect in product(behaviours, repeat=m):
        if is_conscious(list(inspect), m, b):
            found_conscious = True
    print(f"states={m}, observations={b}, behaviours={len(behaviours)}")
    print(f"Any conscious (surjective) self-model found? {found_conscious}")
    print("Expected: False -- surjection onto a strictly larger set is impossible.\n")


def demo_diagonal_witness() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("A concrete un-inspected behaviour (diagonal witness)")
    print("=" * 68)
    m, b = 3, 2
    # An arbitrary inspection map: state i models everything as observation i%2.
    inspect = [tuple((i + j) % b for j in range(m)) for i in range(m)]
    beta = diagonal_witness(inspect)
    print("inspection map (state -> behaviour):")
    for i, row in enumerate(inspect):
        print(f"  state {i}: {row}")
    print(f"diagonal witness beta = {beta}")
    print(f"beta equals some state's model? "
          f"{beta in set(inspect)}  (expected: False)\n")


def demo_injective_resolution() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Perfect resolution: an injective self-model always exists")
    print("=" * 68)
    m, b = 4, 2
    inspect = injective_self_model(m, b)
    distinct = len(set(inspect)) == m
    print("injective inspection map (state -> behaviour):")
    for i, row in enumerate(inspect):
        print(f"  state {i}: {row}")
    print(f"All {m} states carry distinct models? {distinct} (expected: True)")
    print(f"Conscious (complete)? {is_conscious(inspect, m, b)} (expected: False)\n")


def demo_coverage_decay() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Coverage fraction decays exponentially: max coverage = m * b^-m")
    print("=" * 68)
    b = 2
    for m in range(1, 11):
        frac = coverage_fraction(m, b)
        print(f"|S|={m:>2}: max representable fraction = {frac:.6e}")
    print()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo_counting_table()
    demo_no_conscious_small()
    demo_diagonal_witness()
    demo_injective_resolution()
    demo_coverage_decay()
